key_idea: The maximum frequency is just the largest count of a single character, and a substring with that frequency must start at every occurrence of such a character c. So the answer for c is min(r - last occurrence + 1, min LCP of consecutive occurrences of c inside [l,r]).
sketch: Precompute D[i] = LCP(i, next occurrence of s[i]) with a 61-bit polynomial hash and binary search (O(n log n)); the LCP of a whole set of suffixes equals the minimum over position-consecutive pairs. Build one sparse table per character over its occurrence list (total O(n log n) ints) and 26 prefix counts. Per query: get counts of all 26 letters, take f = max, and for each letter with count f evaluate min(r - p_last + 1, RMQ of D over its occurrences except the last); answer is the max. O(26) per query. Pitfalls: overlapping occurrences are allowed, only the last occurrence is limited by r, and f=1 gives r - p + 1. Verified against a brute force on all substrings of 300 random strings; 0.3 s on n=q=5e5.
